name: Karajarri
confidence_why: Johnson 1992 (Nangu dialect) describes primary stress on the initial syllable with secondary stress on alternate syllables and Thieberger 1993 says the same for the region generally, but Capell 1962 (coastal Najanaja dialect) places main stress on the penultimate syllable in words of four or more syllables (ˌgali'guru 'boomerang') while agreeing on initial stress in two- and three-syllable words, and since Johnson himself notes that no detailed study of Karajarri stress has been made, initial stress is the likely reading but its placement in longer words is unsettled.
catalog_citation: (1) Johnson, Edward. 1992. Karajarri sketch grammar. BA (Hons) thesis, Department of Linguistics, University of Sydney. ii+130 pp. Open Access, ANU Open Research Repository hdl:1885/277329 (Nangu dialect, Bidyadanga/La Grange 1992). (2) Capell, A. 1962. Some linguistic types in Australia (Handbook of Australian Languages, Part 2). Oceania Linguistic Monographs 7. Sydney: University of Sydney. 'Garadjari Grammar' pp. 51-89, section 1.5 'Stress' (coastal = Najanaja dialect), read in the Rosetta Project excerpt archive.org.
catalog_locator: Johnson 1992: ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.3 'Stress and intonation', p. 10. Capell 1962: 'Garadjari Grammar', sec. 1.5 'Stress', p. 2 of the Rosetta Project excerpt 'Karadjeri Phonology' (monograph page number cropped; section lies within pp. 54-60).
catalog_quote: JOHNSON 1992, sec. 2.3: "No detailed study of stress has been done in Karajarri, but as is typical of most Australian languages, basic stress patterns can be described by the following principles (Dixon, 1980): primary stress occurs on the initial syllable of a word, and secondary stress sometimes (though less common in rapid speech) on the third, fifth etc. syllables. A typical sentence form one of the texts, for example, has roughly the following stress pattern (this sentence is from text A.1.1): yánu pála jálangkà ngájukura pírra kúwikàrti" -- CAPELL 1962, sec. 1.5: "b) Stress tends to fall on the penultimate in words of two syllables: /'marŋu/ 'man', /'djandu/ 'woman'. c) In words of three syllables the stress is on the first: /'gangara/ 'up'; /'ŋanagu/ 'for what?'; /'wanadi/ 'it is'. Even /'wandi/ is heard for the last word. d) A long vowel carries the stress: /bi'la:wila/ 'a sole'. e) Words of more than three syllables usually carry the main stress on the penultimate, with subsidiary stress on the fourth or fifth syllable from the end: /ˌganbalgu'jaŋan/ 'we'll cook it'; /ˌgali'guru/ 'boomerang'; /ˌwaŋa'laŋu/ 'young men'; /ˌmira-'riŋgu ˌgawa'bula/ 'in-the-hand carry-them-two'."

new_statements.locator: Chapter 2 Phonology, section 2.3 'Stress and intonation', p. 10 (PDF page 20)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (140-page ANU scan) and rendered PDF page 20 (printed p. 10). Section 2.3 'STRESS AND INTONATION' reads exactly as quoted: 'No detailed study of stress has been done in Karajarri, but as is typical of most Australian languages, basic stress patterns can be described by the following principles (Dixon, 1980): primary stress occurs on the initial syllable of a word, and secondary stress sometimes (though less common in rapid speech) on the third, fifth etc. syllables. A typical sentence form one of the texts, for example, has roughly the following stress pattern (this sentence is from text A.1.1): yánu pála jálangkà ngájukura pírra kúwikàrti'. The page…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word; secondary stresses may fall on odd-numbered following syllables (3rd, 5th), i.e. left-to-right alternating rhythm, secondary stresses often suppressed in fast speech.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Johnson: secondary stress 'sometimes' on the third, fifth etc. syllables, less common in rapid speech (example jálangkà, kúwikàrti). Capell 1962 instead places a 'subsidiary stress on the fourth or fifth syllable from the end' with MAIN stress on the penult in words of four or more syllables (/ˌganbalgu'jaŋan/, /ˌwaŋa'laŋu/).
new_statements.exceptions: Johnson gives none beyond the rapid-speech caveat and the hedge that no detailed study exists (his principles are explicitly modelled on Dixon 1980). Capell 1962 sec. 1.5 (coastal/Najanaja dialect, saved Rosetta excerpt) gives a partly different set of rules: two- and three-syllable words stressed on the first syllable, but 'Words of more than three syllables usually carry the main stress on the penultimate, with subsidiary stress on the fourth or fifth syllable from the end'; 'A long vowel carries the stress: /bi'la:wila/'; final stress only with the vocative suffix -i/-u or a word-final diphthong (/ŋa'wai/ 'yes'); suffixation does not necessarily shift stress (/ga'rimba/, /ga'rimbagu/; /'banagagu/); compounds may or may not keep element stresses. Capell's own examples include /ˌgali'guru/ 'boomerang' and /ga'rimba/ with non-initial main stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Johnson's statement is about the word; his illustration is a stress-marked sentence from a recorded Nangu-dialect text, every word initial-stressed. Capell's penultimate 'main stress' in long words and phrases (e.g. /ˌmira-'riŋgu ˌgawa'bula/) may reflect phrase-level prominence in his coastal-dialect text material; neither author separates word stress from phrasal accent instrumentally. The closest relative Nyangumarta is described by Sharp 2004 (PL 556, sec. 2.6) as initial primary stress with alternating rhythm and no final stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both statements are Karadjeri/Karajarri (kara1476, gbd) but different dialects: Johnson 1992 describes the Nangu ('middle') dialect as spoken at Bidyadanga (La Grange) in 1992; Capell 1962 describes the coastal dialect (Najanaja/'nadja', Beagle Bay Mission informants). Karajarri has three named varieties (Najanaja coastal, Nangu, Nawurtu inland), all mutually intelligible per Johnson; I did not verify Glottolog dialect-level codes for them. The Sharp 2004 PL-556 file saved in the folder is Nyangumarta (nyan1301), a sister Marrngu language, kept only as labelled comparative material.

new_statements.quote: Word stress is usually on the first syllable, so it is the first part of the word that sounds the loudest. For example, in the English word 'radio', stress occurs on the first part of the word 'radio', in 'retire' stress occurs in the second part of the word.
new_statements.citation: Thieberger, Nicholas (1996). Handbook of Western Australian Aboriginal Languages South of the Kimberley Region. Pacific Linguistics, Australian National University.
new_statements.locator: Section 1.5.1 'Pronunciation guide' (introduction), printed p. 6, p. 14 (general remark for Western Australian languages); Karajarri entry 4.5.1, pp. 156-159, pp. 164-167 (bibliographic only)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (416 pp.); extracted text of p. 14 = printed p. 6, section 1.5.1 'Pronunciation guide' (header on p. 13), reads exactly: 'Word stress is usually on the first syllable, so it is the first part of the word that sounds the loudest. For example, in the English word 'radio', stress occurs on the first part of the word 'radio', in 'retire' stress occurs in the second part of the word.' Verbatim. It is a guide to the practical spelling system for Western Australian languages generally, not a Karajarri statement. Karajarri entry 4.5.1 (printed pp. 156-159, pp. 164-167) checked in full: location, 11 name variants, Marrngu classification (AIATSIS A.64), three dialects (Naja/Murgud coastal, Nga…
new_statements.relation_note: The listed open_url (Coombs online edition, contents.htm) returns HTTP 404; the Internet Archive has a 2014-02-19 capture but web.archive.org refused TCP connections by automated download on ports 80 and 443 (three tries). The same work in its 1993 print edition was already held by the project as the ANU text; I downloaded the full ANU PDF (19.2 MB) to verify page numbers. The initial-stress remark agrees with the existing Johnson 1992 statement (primary stress on the initial syllable) but only as a region-wide generalization; for Karajarri itself the handbook is silent, so it adds no independent evidence.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A single general sentence in the handbook's pronunciation guide: in Western Australian Aboriginal languages word stress is 'usually' on the first syllable. It is a regional default, not a statement about Karajarri; the Karajarri entry (4.5.1, pp. 156-159) gives location, names, dialects (Naja/Murgud coastal, Ngangu middle, Nawurtu/Ngaudu inland), speaker numbers, researchers, orthography note ('same as for Nyangumarta and Martu Wangka') and a bibliography, with no phonology or stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Thieberger 1993/1996 lists three Karajarri dialects: Naja or Murgud (coastal), Ngangu (middle), Nawurtu (McGregor) / Ngaudu (McKelson) (inland). His stress remark is not tied to any dialect (or to Karajarri). The existing Johnson 1992 statement describes the Nangu dialect (per our earlier reading's). Sands 1989, per Thieberger's bibliography, is 'a grammar based on Laves's Karajarri material' (Laves fieldwork 1929-31, Karadjeri).
